DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
The study asks Cabinet to approve a district-wide weekly food waste service from April 2027, at a net cost of about £490,000 a year, which it says is fully covered by a provisional £520,000 new-burdens allocation. It rests on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households, a projection of 3,290 tonnes a year, and treatment at Brookfield, 14 miles away.

The cost arithmetic is correct and the pilot is good evidence. But three findings in the document's own tables undercut its conclusions:
- the housing-type result is the opposite of what the text says;
- the projection uses a participation rate that doesn't appear in the pilot data;
- Brookfield's capacity covers just over half the projected tonnage.

Once these are corrected, "fully funded" no longer holds.

## 1. Participation was not similar across houses and flats

| Housing type | Participation |
|---|---|
| Houses | **66%** |
| Flats | **21%** |

Flats participated at about a third of the rate of houses. The text calls this "broadly similar," the recommendation relies on it, and your description repeats it. The data support the opposite conclusion: **flats need a different approach.** Typical options are communal containers, different caddies and targeted communications. The pilot gave flats a 23-litre *outdoor* caddy, which may be part of the problem.

## 2. The projection uses a participation rate that doesn't exist in the pilot

- §3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate." Table 1 gives **57%** overall: 66% for houses, 21% for flats. I can't find where 64% comes from.
- Projecting each housing type separately, using the district's 20% flats share (the same as the pilot's):

| | Households | Participating | kg per week | Tonnes a year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 27,456 | 1.9 | 2,713 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 2,184 | 1.4 | 159 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | 29,640 | | **about 2,870** |

That is about 13% below the 3,290 tonnes used throughout the study. The pilot ran January to June, so seasonal variation and novelty effects could move the real figure either way.

## 3. Brookfield can't take the projected tonnage

- §4 says Brookfield offers **up to 1,800 tonnes a year** until an expansion planned for 2029. Both the study's 3,290 tonnes and the corrected 2,870 tonnes exceed this, by about 1,500 or 1,070 tonnes respectively.
- The excess has to go somewhere. The next AD plant is 46 miles away, with no gate fee or haulage cost given.
- The full £74-a-tonne saving is therefore guaranteed only on 1,800 tonnes, about **£133,000**, not £243,000.
- "Treatment is local" (your description) is true for only part of the waste. The 2029 expansion is planned, not certain.

## 4. What this does to the funding

The cost table's arithmetic is correct. Six vehicles × £165,000 ÷ 7 = £141,400; crews £408,000; total £733,400; net £490,400 on the study's own figures.

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net cost | Against £520,000 allocation |
|---|---|---|---|
| As stated (3,290 t, all at Brookfield) | £243,000 | £490,000 | £30,000 spare |
| Corrected tonnage, ignoring capacity limit | £212,500 | £521,000 | **About £1,000 short** |
| Corrected tonnage, saving only on Brookfield's 1,800 t | £133,000 + saving on the rest, less haulage | Up to £600,000 | **Short by up to £80,000** |

The correction to tonnage alone removes the margin. Add the capacity limit and the service needs more than the allocation, by an amount that depends on the second plant's costs.

## 5. Costs that aren't in Table 2

Your description says "every cost line is shown." These are missing or unclear:
- **The dedicated phone line and web page** described in §6.
- **Cover for sickness and holidays.** Six crews with no relief staff, and no spare vehicle.
- **Recruitment, training and supervision.**
- **Ongoing liners.** §6 mentions a three-month supply only. Say whether the Council supplies liners after that, and whether the "annualised" line covers it.
- **Capital funding.** Depreciation spreads the cost on paper, but £990,000 must be found by December 2026, or financed with interest. The study doesn't say which.
- **The basis for six vehicles.** That is about 1,730 households per vehicle per day over a five-day week. A round-planning check would show whether that is realistic.

## 6. Points to check, from my own knowledge rather than the document

Hold these at lower weight than everything above.

- **Statutory deadline.** My understanding is that the Simpler Recycling rules required weekly food waste collections in England from 31 March 2026, with transitional arrangements for some councils. If Thornbury has no transitional arrangement, an April 2027 start may already be late. Check this with your policy team.
- **The incineration saving may not be fully realisable.** Many incinerator contracts include minimum-tonnage guarantees. If Thornbury's does, diverting food waste may not save the full £112 a tonne. Check the contract.
- **New-burdens funding.** It is described as provisional. Its amount and duration should be confirmed before the Council relies on it.

## 7. What holds up

- **The pilot itself:** a sensible size, a deliberate mix of housing types, and participation measured weekly. This is good local evidence.
- **House participation of 66%** at 1.9 kg a week is a solid, usable figure.
- **Low contamination** (under 2% in spot checks) and falling missed-collection reports.
- **The disposal unit costs** use real figures: the actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee.
- **The timeline** works back sensibly from the vehicle lead time, though it has no contingency if vehicles arrive late.
- **Resident satisfaction.** The 81% rating is positive, but the survey response rate isn't given, and participating households are the most likely to respond.

## 8. What is settled and what is open

**Settled by the document's own figures:**
- flats participated at a much lower rate than houses;
- the 64% rate doesn't come from the pilot;
- projected tonnage exceeds Brookfield's contracted capacity;
- on corrected figures, the allocation doesn't cover the net cost.

**Open, and what would settle each question:**

| Question | What would settle it |
|---|---|
| Cost of treating the surplus tonnage | A quote from the 46-mile plant, plus haulage costing |
| The right service for flats | A short trial of communal containers or adapted caddies |
| Missing operating costs | A full operating budget, including cover and the phone line |
| Whether the incineration saving is realisable | The incinerator contract's minimum-tonnage terms |
| Status of the new-burdens funding | Confirmation of the amount and duration |
| Statutory deadline | Checking Thornbury's status under the Simpler Recycling rules |

## 9. Suggested revision to the recommendation

> The pilot shows good participation in houses (66%) but low participation in flats (21%), so flats will need a tailored service. Projected tonnage is about 2,870 tonnes a year, above Brookfield's contracted capacity of 1,800 tonnes until 2029. On corrected figures, the net cost is at or above the provisional £520,000 allocation, depending on the cost of treating the surplus elsewhere. We recommend that Cabinet authorise the vehicle order to protect the April 2027 start, and ask officers to report back by [date] with surplus treatment costs, a flats service design and a full operating budget, before approving the roll-out.

I can rebuild the cost table with these scenarios set out side by side, if that would help.
